title: Localize While You Build: How 6 Global Teams Ship Email in Up to 127 Locales
summary: How to build and translate marketing emails with AI. Compare tool types, follow 5 steps, and see how teams manage 127+ locales from one template.
body_markdown:
**The best way to build and translate marketing emails with AI is to do both in the same place.**


A small confession from the email world: most global teams still translate email with a spreadsheet.


Build it in English. Export the copy. Wait. Paste it back, one locale at a time. Test. Find the German button that wrapped onto three lines. Fix it. Do Japanese. (Then someone changes the English subject line, and you start over.)


Teams aren't short on translation tools. The problem is that email is a strange, stubborn format, and most translation tools were never built for it. Translation tools handle the words. Email builders handle the design. Email localization needs both.


Here's our take: localize while you build, not after. When translation is the last step, every late edit sends you back to the queue, and every new market means a new copy of every template. When localization is part of the build, you translate each block once, lock the approved email, and ship every language the same day as the English. The six teams below made exactly that switch, and their numbers show what it's worth.


Dyspatch is an enterprise email production platform that lets teams build emails with a no-code builder or an AI agent, translate them with AI or their own translation vendor, and manage 300+ locales from a single template, with approvals and sync to their sending platform built in.


Key takeaways


- Email localization is more than translation. It covers layout, legal copy, approvals and sending, in every locale.
- The fastest teams localize while they build: they translate shared blocks once, lock approved emails, and ship every language the same day as the English.
- Translation tools handle words and email builders handle design. Email-native platforms like Dyspatch do both, with AI translation and integrations for Smartling, Phrase, XTM and Crowdin.
- Real results: Culture Amp went from about 800 templates to about 80 across 45 languages, and a Fortune 500 company cut localized time to market from 2 to 3 months to 17 days.
- It affects revenue: 56% of multilingual U.S. shoppers have walked away from a purchase over poor localization (Liferay, 2026).


Quick quiz


#### How long did one localized email take to finish?


A Fortune 500 consumer electronics company sends email in 127+ locales. Before Dyspatch, how long did it take to get one internationalized email template to market?


**D, two to three months. For one template.** Fifteen steps, siloed teams, a developer on every change, and a new version of every template for every new market. Today it takes 17 days for design, translation, testing and review, and often just a few.


(C was the "after." Gold star if you picked it.)


Bonus round


#### What share of multilingual U.S. shoppers have walked away from a purchase because a site or app felt poorly adapted to their language?


**56%.** That's from[Liferay's 2026 Website Localization Report](https://www.liferay.com/w/56-of-multilingual-consumers-have-walked-away-from-a-purchase-over-poor-website-localization-liferay-survey-finds) , a survey of 800 U.S. adults fielded in September 2026.


The kicker: 54% of people who rated the translations as good or excellent still walked away. Being accurate isn't enough. It has to feel like it was written for them.


## What is email localization?


Email localization is adapting an email's copy, images, layout, offers and legal content for a recipient's language, region and culture. Translation is one part of it. Localization also covers how the email looks, what it's allowed to say in each country, who approves it and how it gets sent.


## Why is email localization harder than translation?


Translation changes the words. Email localization has to change the words without breaking everything around them:


- **Layouts break.** German and French copy often runs longer than English, and right-to-left languages like Arabic and Hebrew flip the whole design.
- **Shared copy multiplies.** One legal footer can live in hundreds of templates. Translate it per template, and you pay for the same sentence hundreds of times.
- **Versions drift.** One late edit to the English, and every locale is quietly out of date.
- **Approvals scatter.** Legal in one country, brand in another, a regional marketer in a third, each looking at a different version.
- **Every locale still has to ship.** Personalization and conditional content need to survive the trip to your sending platform, in every language.


## Why should localization be part of the email build, not a project at the end?


Because the expensive part of localization isn't the translating. It's everything that happens around it: exporting, waiting, pasting, retesting and starting over when the English changes. Most teams still run localization as a project that starts once the English is approved. The teams that scale treat it as part of how email gets built.


- **It lives where the work happens.** Translation is a step in the same workspace as design and approval, not a handoff to another team and another tool.
- **It connects to the tools you already use.** Designs come in from Figma, strings go out to your translation system, finished emails sync to your sending platform, and AI agents build through an MCP server.
- **It never falls behind.** A change to one block flows to every template and every language, so the translations always match the source.
- **It lets small teams go global early.** Hunter Industries runs international email with two people. Two Wombats grew from 4 to 16 languages without duplicating every email per language.


That last point is the one we care about most. When localization is a project, going global is something only big teams can afford. When it's built in, a team of two can launch a new market the same week as the English.


## What are the top AI tools for building and translating marketing emails?


It depends on where your bottleneck is. There are four types of tools, and each solves a different part of the job:


Tool type Great at Falls short on Best for


**Machine translation engines** Fast, low-cost first drafts of copy Building, rendering or approving email Translating text you'll paste somewhere else


**Translation management systems** Translator workflows, glossaries, translation memory They see strings, not email layouts Localization teams covering many content types


**Email builders** Drag-and-drop design Usually one language per template, no translation workflow Teams sending in one language


**Email-native localization platforms, like Dyspatch** Building, translating, approving and syncing emails in one place Needs a modular block library and someone to own it Teams sending in 5+ locales, or sending weekly


Most enterprise teams don't pick just one. They connect their translation management system to Dyspatch, so translators keep their tools and email teams keep theirs.


## What should you look for in an AI email localization tool?


Seven things to check before you buy:


1. **Native email rendering.** Preview every locale in the real email layout, not in a strings file.
2. **Block-level translation.** Translate shared content once and reuse it across every template.
3. **Translation choice.** Built-in AI translation plus integrations with the translation management system you already use.
4. **Approvals and locking.** Lock approved emails so translations always match the final version.
5. **Layouts that flex.** Templates that survive long German or Hungarian copy and right-to-left languages.
6. **Sending-platform sync.** Export each locale to your sending platform with personalization intact.
7. **Agent access.** An MCP server or API, so AI assistants build emails inside your brand rules instead of around them.


Test any tool against your hardest email, not its demo template. A legal-heavy transactional email in your longest language will tell you more than any feature list.


## How do you build and translate emails at scale? 5 steps


1. **Build with reusable blocks.** Turn footers, headers, legal copy and company blurbs into blocks. Translate each one once, and reuse it in every template.
2. **Lock the email once it's approved.** Translators work from the final version, and nobody edits under them.
3. **Send strings to translation, not screenshots.** Use Dyspatch's[AI translation](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/ai-for-marketers/) , which reads context and keeps your brand voice. Or connect Smartling, Phrase, XTM or Crowdin, or export standard POT/PO files for any vendor. Either way, translations land back in the template.
4. **Preview and[approve](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/email-collaboration/) every locale.** Check layout and legal copy locale by locale, with comments right on the email.
5. **Sync to your sending platform.** Export each locale with conditional content converted to your platform's format.


**Bonus step: let your agent draft it.** Through the Dyspatch[MCP server](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/mcp-agent-operators-in-dyspatch/) , AI assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude can build an email in Dyspatch from a plain-language brief, using your blocks, brand guardrails and localizations. Try "Build our welcome email in French, Spanish and Japanese" and see how close the first draft lands.

- **A Fortune 500 electronics company:** 127+ locales and 250% faster time to market.


### Culture Amp: 800 templates down to about 80


Culture Amp's people platform serves 25 million employees at more than 6,500 companies, in 45 languages. Their transactional emails used to live as code in a Git repository, roughly 800 templates once you counted every localized copy, and every update needed an engineer. Today they run about 80 main templates built from five base templates, translate and test through their Smartling integration in one place, and ship new emails in hours or days instead of weeks. Product teams build email without waiting on design or engineering, and design approves every module before it goes live.


[Read the Culture Amp story →](https://www.dyspatch.io/blog/how-culture-amp-uses-dyspatch-to-build-employee-experiences-in-45-languages/)


### Hairburst: 11 territories, 9 languages, zero design briefs


Hairburst's CRM team sends in nine languages, including Romanian, Czech, Slovak and Hungarian. Before Dyspatch, an in-house team translated every email by hand, bespoke designs broke after translation (Hungarian runs a lot longer than English), and sends were stitched together with spreadsheets. Now they translate with AI, build from approved modules and ship 10x faster. Black Friday went from a month of lead time to same-day builds. Rory Armitage-Burns, Head of Data, Platforms and AI, put it simply: "It makes the process of building out emails across 11 territories in nine languages a lot more straightforward."

Two Wombats runs a subscription business scaling across Europe, in a regulated market where a language error carries real risk. Instead of duplicating every email per language and re-checking compliance each time, Dave Walker, Head of Growth, went with block-level localization and grew from 4 to 16 languages. The line from their story we keep coming back to: treat localization as an operating system, not a checkbox.

With Dyspatch and a direct Smartling integration, they now send in 12 languages, and more than 20 non-technical teammates manage templates themselves. David Vallejo, Director of Product Management, says the team has "eliminated deployments for simple changes." And Adriana Valencia, the Product Manager leading globalization, sums up the goal: supporting users "in their language, on their terms."

Before Dyspatch, they pasted translations in from spreadsheets, spent 20 minutes per language before any testing, and struggled to control translation costs on even small edits. The team from our quiz cut its email workflow from 15 steps to 10. Each team got its own workspace inside one shared design system, and they now send a single block for translation instead of a whole template. ## Can AI translate marketing emails accurately?


For first drafts and most transactional emails, yes, especially when the AI has context and knows your brand voice. For legal copy and high-stakes campaigns, keep a human reviewer in the approval step. Readers notice the difference: in the same[Liferay survey](https://www.liferay.com/w/56-of-multilingual-consumers-have-walked-away-from-a-purchase-over-poor-website-localization-liferay-survey-finds) , 82% said they're confident they can spot machine-translated content, and only 20% credited AI alone for strong localization, versus 43% who credited human involvement. In Dyspatch, AI translation and human review run in the same workflow, so you don't have to choose.


## Does email localization actually pay off?


Yes, if you sell outside your home language. In[Liferay's 2026 Website Localization Report](https://www.liferay.com/w/56-of-multilingual-consumers-have-walked-away-from-a-purchase-over-poor-website-localization-liferay-survey-finds) (800 U.S. adults who had used a non-English website or app in the past year, surveyed in September 2026), 56% had decided not to buy because a site or app felt poorly adapted to their language, and 48% had picked a competitor that fit their language and culture better. Only 23% said non-English websites usually feel written for them. The survey covers websites and apps, not email, but email is often the first thing those customers read from you, so the same bar applies.


## Do you need an email localization platform?


Honest answer: not always.


- **Probably not** if you send in one or two languages, a few times a year, with a translator you trust and a spreadsheet you don't hate.
- **Probably yes** if you send in five or more locales, send weekly or triggered emails, have legal copy that varies by country, have more than one team building email, or want AI agents building emails without breaking your brand.


## What to do this week


1. **Count your re-translations.** Pull last quarter's translation invoices and look for sentences you paid for more than once. Footers are usually the worst offender.
2. **Map your steps.** Write down every handoff for one localized email, from brief to send. More than 10? There's room to cut.
3. **Start with your busiest template.** Turn its shared copy into blocks, lock it, and translate once.
4. **Hand it to an agent.** Give your AI assistant a three-language brief and judge the first draft.
